summaries.example: Imagine a machine that can move only when something pushes it. More asked whether everything in nature was like that. He thought matter was passive, like the machine, and that souls or other spirits were needed to explain living movement. He also compared space to a huge, invisible room in which every body and spirit exists.
summaries.summary: Henry More tried to join careful reasoning, Christianity, and the new science of his time. He agreed that matter and motion explained many natural events, but he thought they could not explain everything. In his view, matter was passive, while souls and other spirits could begin activity. He called one helping power the Spirit of Nature. More also argued that space was real and infinite, and that even spirits had to exist in space. His moral and religious ideas were unusual. He thought good and evil were real standards that even God followed, and therefore God created the best possible world. More wanted religion to be guided by reason, but his strong belief in spiritual happenings and his special theories made some other thinkers doubt his arguments. His ideas later influenced discussions about space, science, religion, and the soul.
key_ideas: Henry More was a seventeenth-century English philosopher and theologian linked with the Cambridge Platonists.
He used reason and ideas from new mechanical science to defend souls, spirits, and belief in God.
He thought matter could not act by itself, so an immaterial Spirit of Nature helped explain things such as gravity, growth, and animal movement.
More believed that space and time were real and that everything that exists must exist somewhere and sometime.
He supported a broad Christian approach in which only a few teachings were essential, but he also held unusual views about souls and religion.
summaries.why_it_matters: More shows how one thinker tried to answer big questions using both science and religion. His work helps us see that people can agree about some evidence but disagree about what it means. It also raises lasting questions about whether physical explanations are enough, how minds relate to bodies, and whether moral truths depend on anyone’s wishes.

important_terms.definition: The view that mind or soul and body are two different kinds of reality.
The idea that nature can give us reasons for believing in God.
More’s name for an invisible, active power between God and physical things.
The belief that moral truths, such as good and evil, exist independently of anyone’s choice.

questions_to_think_about: Can a machine ever be alive, or does life require something more?
If science explains many events by matter and motion, should we still look for other kinds of explanations?
Would a perfectly good God have to create the best possible world?
What makes a religious belief reasonable?

summaries.example: Suppose a physical theory explains how moving particles collide but does not explain why a plant develops, why a magnet attracts, or why gravity operates as it does. More would say that the theory has reached its limit and that an immaterial active principle is required. He called this principle the Spirit of Nature. A critic such as Robert Boyle could reply that an extra spirit merely fills a gap in explanation without showing that it exists.
summaries.summary: Henry More was a theologian and philosopher associated with the Cambridge Platonists, though his system was highly individual. He adopted much of the mechanical philosophy associated with Descartes, especially its account of matter as passive, but he argued that mechanical interactions could not explain all natural phenomena. Since activity, in his view, belonged properly to immaterial substance, he proposed the Spirit of Nature as a blind, pervasive, secondary cause operating between God and the material world. More’s account of spirit differed from Cartesian dualism because he held that every real entity, including God, souls, and spirits, must exist in space. In his Manual of Metaphysics, infinite space became a central example of immaterial reality and was described as closely connected with divine attributes. More also developed necessitarian theology: eternal standards of goodness and conceptual order constrain God, so God must create the best possible world. This opposed voluntarist and Calvinist views that emphasize God’s unconstrained will. More supported religious tolerance about nonessential doctrines, yet his unusual views about souls, prophecy, spiritual phenomena, and Kabbalah made his position difficult to classify. His contemporaries disputed both his natural philosophy and his theology, while later thinkers, especially Newton, found some of his ideas about space and time important even though they did not accept the Spirit of Nature.
key_ideas: More began by welcoming Cartesian mechanical philosophy, but he always disputed parts of Descartes’s account of space, body, animal life, and causation.
His mature dualism defined body as passive and physically divisible, while spirit was active, extended, and not physically separable.
The Spirit of Nature was meant to be a secondary, blind, non-intelligent cause that supplied what matter-and-motion explanations could not.
More argued that infinite space and duration were real and that existence required a location in space; this differed sharply from Descartes’s view that souls are non-spatial.
His ethical and theological rationalism held that goodness and justice are eternal standards to which God necessarily conforms.
More’s theories were challenged by figures including Boyle, Hooke, Hale, Baxter, and others, who questioned his physics or his account of divine freedom.
summaries.why_it_matters: More is important for the history of philosophy because he stood at a crossroads between Platonism, Christianity, and early modern science. His work makes visible a central question: when a mechanical explanation is incomplete, should we introduce a nonmaterial cause or seek a better physical account? His theories also show that ideas about space, divine power, moral objectivity, and scientific method can shape one another. Later debates about Newton, Locke, materialism, and religious rationalism continued to engage problems that More had formulated.

important_terms.definition: The position that body and soul, or matter and spirit, are fundamentally different kinds of substance.
A seventeenth-century approach that sought evidence for God from nature, reason, and the order of the world.
More’s immaterial but spatially extended secondary cause, supposed to organize or activate matter under general laws of nature.
The view that matter is passive or inert and that genuine activity belongs to immaterial entities.
More’s position that moral and conceptual principles exist eternally and necessarily constrain God’s creative choice.
The view that God freely chooses how to create and is not limited by pre-existing moral standards.
More’s theory of infinite, real, three-dimensional space, treated as an example of immaterial substance and closely related to God.
More’s distinction between what can be physically torn into parts and a spirit, which may be extended but cannot be physically divided.

questions_to_think_about: Does identifying an unexplained phenomenon establish a new kind of substance, or only show that a theory is incomplete?
Can an entity be extended in space without being physically divisible?
Would a perfectly good God be free to create a world worse than the best possible one?
Is a theory more convincing when it unifies science and theology, or can that combination create new problems?
Why might More’s close associates Anne Conway and John Finch have rejected important parts of his philosophy?

summaries.example: Think about a wind-up toy. Its wheels move because parts push other parts. More believed that many physical events could work in a similar mechanical way, but he did not think this explained a growing plant or an animal moving on its own. He said matter could receive motion but could not truly begin activity. He therefore proposed an invisible Spirit of Nature that worked throughout the world without thinking or planning each event.
summaries.summary: Henry More was a seventeenth-century English philosopher and theologian connected with the Cambridge Platonists. He wanted Christianity to agree with reason, and he used the new mechanical philosophy associated with Descartes as part of that project. Mechanical philosophy explained nature through matter, motion, and laws. More accepted much of it, but he believed matter was completely passive and could not begin activity. To explain what mechanics seemed unable to explain, he proposed the Spirit of Nature, an immaterial power that operated throughout the world. He also defended a strong body-soul dualism. For More, spirit was not an invisible point with no location: everything real had to exist in space, including souls and God. In his later work, he treated infinite space as an especially clear example of immaterial reality and connected it with divine attributes. More’s ethics and theology were necessitarian. He believed goodness and justice were eternal, so God necessarily created the best possible world rather than choosing moral rules arbitrarily. He also supported Latitudinarianism, which sought agreement on a few essential Christian teachings while allowing variation elsewhere. Critics argued that More’s Spirit of Nature was unnecessary, that his experiments and physics were mistaken, or that his theology limited divine power. His influence continued through later debates about space, time, science, religion, and materialism.
key_ideas: More lived at Cambridge and became an important early teacher of Cartesian philosophy in Britain.
He thought Descartes’s mechanical science was powerful but limited: matter and motion could not explain every natural event.
More’s Spirit of Nature was supposed to explain activities such as gravity, magnetism, growth, and the movement of living things.
Unlike Descartes, More said spirits and God were extended in space, although spirits could not be physically cut into pieces.
He argued that God’s perfect goodness required God to choose what was best, so morality was not created simply by divine choice.
More favored religious peace about many disputed doctrines, but his own theories about souls, prophecy, and spiritual events were often unusual.
summaries.why_it_matters: More helps us understand why early modern thinkers did not always see science and religion as separate subjects. He hoped scientific reasoning would defend belief in souls and God, but his arguments also provoked criticism from scientists and theologians. Studying him gives us practice comparing explanations, distinguishing evidence from interpretation, and asking whether a theory’s religious purpose makes its philosophical claims stronger or weaker.

important_terms.definition: The belief that body and soul are different kinds of substance rather than two versions of the same thing.
Using observations about nature and reasoning to argue for God or divine qualities.
More’s invisible, active helper between God and the physical world.
The claim that physical matter cannot start action by itself.
The belief that good and evil are fixed standards, not rules made true only by God’s decision.
The view that God must follow eternal moral and rational standards when creating the world.
A broad religious approach that treats only a small number of teachings as necessary and allows disagreement about others.
The idea that space exists independently and is large enough for everything physical and spiritual to occupy.

questions_to_think_about: If a scientific explanation leaves something unexplained, what kinds of answers are reasonable?
Could something occupy space without being made of ordinary matter?
Should God be able to choose any action, or must a good God follow moral standards?
Why might people who admire a teacher later reject that teacher’s main ideas?
Can a religion be tolerant while its members still argue strongly about truth?
